quests.scenarioScene: List the feature and the benefit separately in this sentence: 'Our thermostat learns your schedule and adjusts automatically, so you save on heating without thinking about it.'

quests.scenarioScene: This pitch leads with three features and no benefit: 'It has voice control, a mobile app, and geofencing.' Rewrite it leading with the single strongest benefit those features add up to.

quests.explanation: Multiple features often collapse into one real benefit - naming that benefit is more useful than listing the features that produce it.

quests.scenarioScene: A candidate keeps listing features about themselves in an interview: 'I know Python, SQL, and Tableau.' Turn that list into a benefit-led pitch for a hiring manager who mentioned messy reporting.

quests.correctAnswer: I can take your messiest spreadsheet and turn it into a report your team actually trusts by Friday.
quests.explanation: Skills are features. What a manager hires for is the outcome those skills produce for their specific problem.

quests.scenarioScene: When is it stronger to open with the solution instead of the problem?

quests.correctAnswer: When the listener already clearly feels the problem, and stating it again would waste time they don't need to spend.
quests.explanation: Problem-first isn't always the right order - if the problem is already obvious to the listener, leading with the solution respects their time.
